tldr: When robots search for objects using depth maps predicted from monocular RGB images by foundation models, view-dependent errors accumulate and block passages, cutting off exploration. ERA solves this via a mutual feedback mechanism called "Move with Error"—moving to fix errors, and using the corrected map to move further.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of ERA. Revisable occupancy (Move2Error), which clears false obstacles from predicted depth using subsequent free-space observations, forms a closed loop with exploration from reachable viewpoints (Error2Move), which selects new viewpoints from reachable free space to resume observation even when frontiers vanish. After finding the target, it verifies it across multiple views before stopping.
overview:
Zero-shot ObjectNav—finding a specified object in an unseen environment—has traditionally required expensive, bulky sensors like LiDAR or depth cameras. Recently, foundation models like Depth Anything have made it possible to estimate accurate depth from monocular RGB images alone. However, directly plugging this predicted depth into traditional mapping pipelines reveals an unexpected pitfall: subtle, view-dependent prediction errors accumulate, thickening walls and blocking hallways on the map. As a result, frontiers (boundaries with unobserved regions) vanish entirely, leaving the robot stranded mid-search.

To address this, the authors propose a new paradigm called "Move with Error." Instead of treating the map purely as a fixed guide for motion, this approach builds a mutually reinforcing feedback loop: moving to new viewpoints tests and corrects geometric map errors, and the corrected map enables the agent to reach even newer viewpoints.

ERA puts this concept into practice with three components: a revisable occupancy grid (Move2Error) that overwrites and clears past false obstacles using subsequent free-space rays, an exploration strategy from reachable viewpoints (Error2Move) that samples observation viewpoints from the known safe region even when frontiers vanish, and a multi-view target verification mechanism. It requires zero training.

Evaluated on standard benchmarks like HM3D and MP3D, ERA achieves state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods without depth sensors. Furthermore, simply integrating its components into VLFM, a representative navigation framework, dramatically boosts success rate from 10.8% to 61.7%. The authors also successfully deployed ERA on a real, life-sized wheeled humanoid robot.
contributions: Identified the failure mechanism where view-dependent errors in predicted depth accumulate into thickened obstacles, eliminate exploration frontiers, and cause the robot to terminate early
Proposed the "Move with Error" paradigm—a mutually reinforcing loop where movement corrects the map and the corrected map enables further movement—along with ERA, a training-free system realizing it

Developed revisable occupancy (Move2Error) that clears past false obstacles using subsequent free-space observations, and exploration from reachable viewpoints (Error2Move) that continues observation across the reachable space even when frontiers vanish

Achieved state-of-the-art results among training-free methods without depth sensors across three benchmarks, demonstrated high portability to existing methods (VLFM, L3MVN) and other depth models, and verified effectiveness on a real robot

sections.heading: Why does predicted depth cause robots to get stuck halfway?
sections.summary: Foundation models that predict depth from RGB images can eliminate depth sensors, but plugging them directly into existing pipelines causes success rates to collapse. Accumulated prediction errors block hallways and frontiers, trapping the robot in a circular failure where it cannot reach new viewpoints to fix the map.
sections.details:
Recent foundation models predicting depth and 3D geometry from images have advanced rapidly, bringing us closer to autonomous navigation using only camera images without dedicated depth sensors. However, a major hurdle remains: replacing measured sensor depth with predicted depth causes robots to stall midway through exploration.

For example, in VLFM—a representative object navigation system—the success rate on HM3D v2 plummets from 68.2% to 10.8%, even though the mean relative depth error is only about 10%. A similar breakdown happens in L3MVN, which uses a different map representation and planner. Why does performance drop so drastically?

The authors found that slight geometric prediction errors from different viewpoints overlap during map integration, causing walls and obstacles to expand thicker than they actually are. As a result, doorways and hallways that are physically clear become blocked on the map, and frontiers—the boundaries into unobserved space—disappear entirely. Without frontiers, the robot concludes there is nowhere left to search and stops.

This creates a circular dependency: fixing the map requires observations from new viewpoints, but the path to reach them is blocked by the corrupted map. To break this loop, the authors propose "Move with Error," an approach where movement tests and corrects the map, and the corrected map resumes motion.

sections.heading: Comparing mapping rules: How errors wipe out frontiers
sections.summary: Feeding predicted depth into existing mapping rules revealed that reachable frontiers vanish in over half the frames. Experiments showed that rules preserving obstacles or clearing space too slowly cannot recover from prediction errors on their own.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Problem Setting
The robot is given only a target category name (e.g., "chair", "sofa"). Sensors are limited to a single monocular RGB camera and wheel odometry (or simulated pose); no depth sensor is used. It operates in a completely training-free (zero-shot) setting without fine-tuning pre-trained models or training on navigation tasks. Navigation succeeds if the agent calls Stop within 1m of the target object.

### 2.2 Diagnosing Existing Systems and Mapping Rules
Feeding the raw output of a depth prediction model (Depth Anything 3) into existing systems causes both VLFM and L3MVN to fail via early stops. To pinpoint the cause, the authors compared how various map integration rules handle predicted depth errors along 120 identical trajectories.

- **Obstacle-accumulating (VLFM, SemExp, SG-Nav, etc.)**: Cells marked as obstacles are permanently kept. Surface offsets across different views accumulate, causing obstacles to expand and completely block passages.
- **Probabilistic updating (ApexNav)**: Updates evidence weights for obstacles and free space, but obstacle evidence outweighs clearing. It takes tens of frames to erase a false positive, failing to clear blockages quickly.
- **Recent-frame reconstruction (equivalent to MVP-Nav)**: Rebuilds maps using only recent frames and discards past frames. While false errors disappear, correct past obstacles are lost as well, and errors still accumulate within the recent window.

Analyzing the percentage of frames where reachable frontiers exist, ground-truth sensor depth maintains frontiers in nearly 100% of frames. With predicted depth, however, existing rules see frontiers completely vanish in 50% to over 90% of all frames. This led to two design requirements: subsequent free-space observations must reliably overwrite past obstacles (Move2Error), and the agent must keep moving to gain new views even if frontiers disappear (Error2Move).

captions.F7: Comparison of mapping rules on the same frame. With measured depth (top left), reachable area (blue) and frontiers are clear. Under existing predicted depth rules (VLFM, ApexNav, L3MVN, etc.), accumulated false obstacles (orange) trap the blue area, wiping out all frontiers. Only the proposed revisable occupancy grid (bottom right) preserves open pathways.

sections.heading: The ERA system: Three pillars for moving while fixing errors
sections.summary: ERA consists of three components: revisable occupancy that clears past obstacles via free-space rays, reachable viewpoint exploration that picks views from reachable space when frontiers are absent, and target verification that checks multi-view geometric consistency before stopping.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Revisable Occupancy (Move2Error)
To correct predicted depth errors over time, each grid cell holds bounded signed evidence $e_m \in [-E, E]$. Free-space rays are cast through the space between the camera and predicted obstacles as well as observed floors, subtracting evidence. Crucially, the evidence bound $E$ and single update increment $\delta$ are set such that $\delta = E/2$. As a result, even a cell saturated as an obstacle in the past is cleared after being observed as free space from new viewpoints just twice in succession.

In addition, areas swept by the robot's own physical footprint are guaranteed free space, so their evidence is hard-reset to $e_m = -E$. Conversely, if a forward step fails due to collision, that obstacle is added to a contact set $\mathcal{K}_t$ to prevent visual false clearing.

### 3.2 Exploration from Reachable Viewpoints (Error2Move)
Even with a revisable map, frontiers may temporarily disappear. ERA therefore stops relying solely on frontiers and instead samples candidate viewpoints $\mathcal{V}_t$ across the entire currently reachable known free space.

The score for each viewpoint $v$ combines the unobserved area visible from it with image feature similarity from VLFM (a semantic value map) and exploration priority. Even when no unobserved space is directly visible, viewpoints within known space are selected. The robot continues moving, views blocked passages from new angles, clears false obstacles, and reopens its own exploration routes.

### 3.3 Target Verification
When approaching a discovered object, relying blindly on single-view predicted depth leads to stopping errors caused by distance misestimations. ERA tracks the candidate object's 3D surface, updating it with recent high-confidence observations as it gets closer. Before issuing a Stop action, it applies a multi-view consistency check: is it detected in the current frame, is it facing the target, is geometric uncertainty low, and does the 3D position match observations from earlier, distinct camera poses? If consistency fails, the robot orbits to another viewpoint to re-verify.

captions.F4: Example of free-space clearing in action. Without clearing (top row), predicted depth errors create a phantom wall (orange) in the hallway at step 60, permanently blocking it. In the proposed method (bottom row), viewing from a different angle at step 85 clears the false obstacle, allowing the agent to successfully pass through at step 96.

sections.heading: Dramatic gains and real-robot deployment
sections.summary: ERA achieved top-tier success rates across HM3D and MP3D among training-free methods without depth sensors. It boosted VLFM's success rate from 10.8% to 61.7%, and successfully powered real-world navigation on a full-sized wheeled humanoid.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup and Baseline Comparison
Experiments were conducted across three major benchmarks on the Habitat simulator: HM3D v1, HM3D v2, and MP3D. Metrics include Success Rate (SR) and Success weighted by Path Length (SPL). The depth model used was Depth Anything 3, with SigLIP2 and SAM 3 handling open-vocabulary detection.

ERA achieved the highest SR and SPL on all benchmarks among training-free methods without depth sensors. On the challenging HM3D v2, it reached an SR of 70.1%, surpassing the previous best method, MVP-Nav (59.4%), by 10.7 points. This performance rivals methods equipped with real sensor depth, such as sensor-based VLFM (68.2% SR).

### 4.2 Portability and Ablations
The two proposed components—revisable occupancy and reachable viewpoint exploration—also act as general-purpose plug-ins. Integrated into VLFM under predicted depth, its SR jumped from 10.8% to 61.7%, recovering to roughly 90% of its sensor-depth baseline. In L3MVN, SR doubled from 29.2% to 59.1%. Swapping the depth model to VGGT showed similar dramatic improvements, confirming the gains are model-agnostic.

Ablation studies showed that disabling free-space clearing caused SR to collapse from 70.1% to 13.9%, while restricting exploration targets to frontiers alone cut SR by more than half to 32.6%, demonstrating that both components are essential.

### 4.3 Real-Robot Deployment
ERA was deployed on an AgiBot Genie G1 wheeled humanoid robot navigating university hallways using only a single monocular RGB head camera and wheel odometry. Across 12 runs targeting chairs, trash cans, and potted plants, the robot successfully stopped within 1m of the goal in 11 trials. In environments where the baseline system failed completely due to vanished frontiers, ERA cleared its own phantom obstacles and reached the targets.

captions.F5: Real-robot experiments on a wheeled humanoid. The top row shows building a predicted depth map purely from RGB images, discovering a chair, and stopping. The bottom row highlights how ERA pushes past false obstacles to reach a trash can, whereas the Base method terminates early after losing its frontiers.

sections.heading: How does this differ from image-space navigation or 3D reconstruction?
sections.summary: Sensorless methods often navigate purely in image feature space or rely on local reconstructions, both struggling with global geometric consistency. ERA stands apart by assuming predicted depth is imperfect and actively using motion to correct the map.
sections.details:
### Zero-Shot Object Navigation
Recent ObjectNav approaches typically combine the semantic reasoning of foundation models with geometric maps (occupancy or semantic grids) built from depth sensors. However, their geometric backbones largely assume accurate, measured depth is always available.

### Navigation Without Depth Sensors
One line of sensorless research—such as PixNav, PanoNav, and Navi-Agent—bypasses geometric maps altogether, making decisions in image space or on topological graphs. While immune to geometric depth errors, they struggle to capture global free space and evaluate long-range reachability accurately.

Conversely, models like DUSt3R and Depth Anything inspired methods that recover geometry from RGB for planning (such as RANGER and MVP-Nav). However, naive integration like RANGER accumulates errors, while rebuilding from only recent frames like MVP-Nav discards valid past information. ERA maintains an explicit global map while actively correcting errors through movement and re-observation.

### Occupancy Grids and Exploration Strategies
While drawing on classic occupancy grid evidence updates and Next-Best-View exploration principles, ERA introduces evidence bounds and reachable viewpoint sampling tailored specifically to handle the blockages and frontier loss unique to predicted depth.

sections.heading: Wrap-up: Autonomous navigation that embraces imperfect geometry
sections.summary: This study uncovered how error accumulation in predicted depth destroys exploration frontiers, and overcame it through the "Move with Error" paradigm that links movement with map correction. It marks an important step toward autonomous robots free from expensive depth sensors.
sections.details:
This paper addressed zero-shot object navigation in unseen environments using a monocular camera and depth foundation models instead of depth sensors. It revealed the underlying mechanism where view-dependent depth errors create phantom walls, wipe out exploration frontiers, and stop robots prematurely.

To overcome this, the proposed "Move with Error" paradigm and the ERA system form a closed loop between clearing false obstacles via free space (Move2Error) and sustaining observation opportunities through reachable viewpoint exploration (Error2Move). This achieved state-of-the-art results on simulation benchmarks and demonstrated reliable RGB-only object navigation on a physical robot.

sections.heading: Appendix: Trajectory comparisons and robustness to odometry drift
sections.summary: The appendix provides qualitative trajectory comparisons showing VLFM stalling at the start under predicted depth, along with data demonstrating ERA's strong resilience against real-world odometry drift.
sections.details:
### Qualitative Trajectory Comparisons with Existing Methods
Appendix D.3 and Figure F10 compare exploration trajectories between original VLFM under predicted depth, VLFM augmented with ERA's two components, and ERA itself. In the original VLFM, initial turning creates false obstacles all around the agent; frontiers vanish, and it gives up near the start position (marked with an X). In contrast, agents with revisable occupancy and reachable viewpoint exploration break out of rooms, navigate hallways, and reach distant targets.

### Robustness to Odometry Drift
While simulator experiments assume ground-truth poses, physical robots inevitably experience odometry drift from wheel slip. Appendix D.1 evaluates ERA under accumulated Gaussian noise per step, yielding an average error of 0.96m and 11.4 degrees at episode end. Under these harsh conditions, ERA retained over 95% of its success rate compared to using perfect ground-truth poses, proving its practical noise tolerance.

captions.F10: Qualitative comparison of trajectories on HM3D v2. VLFM with predicted depth (blue cross) loses frontiers and terminates right after starting. In contrast, VLFM with the proposed components (red) and ERA (green) overcome false blockages, explore widely, and reach the target object (star).

takeaways: Even with advanced depth foundation models, slight view-dependent prediction errors accumulate in the map and eliminate exploration frontiers, making active map-clearing mechanisms indispensable.
Rather than moving based on blind trust in the map, shifting to "Move with Error"—moving to uncover and correct map errors—is key to autonomous navigation with imperfect perceptual models.
When frontiers vanish, sampling new viewpoints across reachable known space and continuing to move allows the robot to self-heal blocked passages and resume exploration.

The proposed map updating (revisable occupancy) and exploration strategy (reachable viewpoint exploration) are highly modular and can be directly applied to various existing navigation frameworks and depth models.
limitations: Relies on externally provided poses and lacks built-in simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) capable of handling severe drift or loop closures.
Exploring known space to clear obstacles when frontiers vanish can increase path length and steps, leading to lower search efficiency (SPL).

Requires running multiple large foundation models (depth prediction, open-vocabulary segmentation) in parallel, creating heavy onboard computational demands (the paper executed these via an external workstation).
